extracted.intended_audience: antiquaries, architects, art historians, and educated readers interested in Gothic architecture, Venetian palaces, and literary criticism of Spenser
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and evaluation of Gothic architectural design and restoration (with Venetian case studies) together with an allegorical/theological reading of the first books of Spenser's Faerie Queene. Emphasises stylistic, documentary, and moral-interpretive criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic as 'Christian' architecture (not necessarily ecclesiastical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic is called 'Christian' architecture rather than 'ecclesiastical'—there is a wide difference; it is the only architecture Christian men should build, but not necessarily tied to church services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying Gothic forms to civil buildings would reduce prejudice against the style; seeing noble Gothic used in a civil building would decide many skeptics at once. The distinction supports using Gothic broadly in Christian society rather than confining it to churches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern capability in Gothic design demonstrated by absence of timidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A good modern Gothic work should be 'free from all signs of timidity or incapacity' in its overall composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate buildings by their general proportion of parts, refinement and piquancy of mouldings, and especially by 'force, vitality, and grace of floral ornament' worked broadly and in a masculine manner. A successful modern example (e.g., Margaret Street church) signals that 'there need be no limits' to future design ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural sculpture must represent contemporary dress and persons
rubrics_metrics.description: No architectural sculpture was ever good for anything which did not represent the dress and persons of the people living at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If figure-sculpture depicts anachronistic dress it will be ineffective; because modern dress will not form appropriate decorations for spandrils and niches, absence of suitable contemporary models means figure-sculpture will remain inferior for the present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence achievable in floral sculpture, inlaid work, and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Floral sculpture, refinement of inlaid work, and general execution are areas where modern practice may surpass existing Gothic work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if figure-sculpture is presently weak, floral ornament and inlay may be taken much farther; these elements are emphasized as proper fields to demonstrate superior workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of admitting simple workmen to develop skilled artisans
rubrics_metrics.description: The glory of Gothic architecture is to receive the rudest work; admitting the handling of the simplest workman will produce 'many of our simple workmen become cunning ones.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing simpler crafts to participate will, with the aid of modern wealth and science, cultivate skilled workmanship—leading to ambitious projects done with greater refinement than older exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesize Northern Gothic forms with Italian refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the pure and perfect forms of Northern Gothic and work them out with the refinement of Italian art in the details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine the structural/ornamental purity of English and French 13th-century surface Gothic with Italian subtlety in detail to create buildings that may surpass northern examples in certain respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local botanical ornament as a design ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately resolve to display in architecture the beauty of every flower and herb of the English fields, each by each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it an object of ambition to depict every native tree and blossom in architectural ornament—approached humbly and progressively, accepting help even from feeblest hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to architectural ambition: humility and incremental practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin to approach high architectural aims not ambitiously but in humility, accepting help from the feeblest hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advancement depends on modest, collective effort and gradual improvement rather than grand, overreaching designs that current workmanship cannot sustain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic criteria for dating and attributing architectural work
rubrics_metrics.description: Use internal stylistic evidence—mouldings, capitals, bases, traceried windows, and workmanship quality—to distinguish relative dates and authorship of palace parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare mouldings and workmanship to securely dated examples (e.g., chapter-house of the Frari) to carry parts back to early fourteenth-century dates; note Byzantine fragments or masculine/noble features as dating signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration quality as a chronological marker
rubrics_metrics.description: Restorations can be recognized and ordered chronologically by their progressive debasement or coarseness of execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify multiple periods of restoration by comparing paired elements in the same window or wall (e.g., one jamb of a window being of a 'first' period and the opposite jamb of a 'second' period). Coarser mouldings and valueless carved heads indicate later, baser restorations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer documentary decrees over chronicle narrative when dating works
rubrics_metrics.description: Use formal decrees and surviving official documents (e.g., council decrees) to fix dates and intentions for building phases, taking them as more trustworthy than popular chronicles when inconsistencies arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where chronicles conflict or are vague, the precise language of decrees (e.g., designating certain facades or 'new palace') should settle questions of scope and sequence of construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple documentary sources to corroborate architectural history
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and compare various chronicles, manuscripts, and decrees to complete evidence respecting main dates and phases of building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although chronicles often repeat each other, assembling the best-accredited entries helps trace changing terminology (e.g., 'Palazzo Nuovo' vs 'Palazzo Vecchio') and clarifies which parts were intended by period decrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegorical/theological reading of Spenser: map personae to virtues and vices
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the Redcrosse Knight and related figures as personifications (e.g., Redcrosse = Holiness/Pietas; Una = Truth; Duessa = Falsehood; Sans Foy = Infidelity; Sans Loy = Lawlessness; Orgoglio = Carnal Pride).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret episodes as moral/theological types: e.g., Holiness separated from Truth encounters Error (learning-based error), Hypocrisy, then Infidelity; Truth separated from Holiness produces violent reform (lion) and is later captured by Lawlessness. Track allegorical sequences to reveal Spenser's theological argument and social/political typology (e.g., Orgoglio as Papal pride).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret events as moral-typological actions with theological referents
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand combats, captivities, and deliverances in the poem as emblematic of theological and moral processes (e.g., Lawlessness bearing Truth captive = those who 'hold the truth in unrighteousness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scriptural/theological analogues (St. Paul's 'adikia', deliverance by Nature/satyrs, the role of Penitence and Mercy) to read narrative turns as commentary on religious, social, and political conditions. Note personified virtues (Humility, Faith, Hope, Charity, Mercy, Obedience, Patience, Zeal, Reverence) and their functional roles in healing and moral restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic description judged by elaboration and nobility of treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages of elaborate and noble description (e.g., the house of Pride) are judged as among the most significant and high-quality parts of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Spenserian descriptive passages for their richness and ability to convey the moral/systemic meaning of the allegory; such descriptions serve as central nodes for the system of virtues and vices and should be read carefully and connected to the wider moral architecture of the poem.
